title: Cell signaling and the cell cycle
note: Cells talk with chemical signals (ligands) that bind receptors and set off relay chains inside the cell. One major outcome is the decision to divide. The cell cycle is interphase (G1, S, G2) followed by mitosis and cytokinesis, and checkpoints run by cyclins and Cdks keep it from moving on until each step is ready.

read.title: From signal to division
text: Most cells in the body divide only when told to. The message often arrives as a growth factor, a protein ligand released by a nearby cell. Because it is water-soluble, it cannot cross the membrane, so it binds a receptor on the cell surface. Many growth factor receptors are receptor tyrosine kinases: binding brings two receptors together, and they add phosphate groups to each other. Relay proteins inside the cell pick up the signal, and a chain of kinases carries it to the nucleus, where genes for cell division switch on.

The cell then moves through its cycle. In G1 it grows. In S it copies its DNA, so each chromosome becomes two identical sister chromatids held together by cohesin. In G2 it prepares for division. Mitosis then separates the copies: chromosomes condense, attach to the spindle at their kinetochores, line up at the center, and are pulled apart when cohesin is cut. Cytokinesis divides the cytoplasm.

At checkpoints the cell pauses to confirm that conditions are right, that DNA is undamaged, and that every chromosome is attached to the spindle. When these controls fail, cells may divide when they should not.
